extracted_claims.text: Article 43 requires that, for high-risk AI systems, the provider follow the conformity assessment procedure set out in Annex VII where harmonised standards or common specifications do not exist or have not been (fully) applied.

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, where the provider has applied harmonised standards (Article 40) or common specifications (Article 41), the provider may choose between conformity assessment based on internal control (Annex VI) or the procedure involving a notified body based on quality management system and technical documentation assessment (Annex VII).

For most high-risk AI systems not falling under point 1 of Annex III, conformity can be demonstrated by the provider itself through an internal/self-assessment procedure (Annex VI), without mandatory third-party certification.

Annex VII describes a third-party conformity assessment procedure combining evaluation of the provider's quality management system (QMS, per Article 17) and review of technical documentation of the high-risk AI system by a notified body.

Under Annex VII point 4.5, where necessary and after other reasonable means have been exhausted, a notified body may, upon reasoned request, be granted access to the training and trained models of the AI system, including relevant parameters, subject to IP and confidentiality protections.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority to derogate from the Article 43 conformity assessment procedure, authorising placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems for a limited time for exceptional reasons of public security, health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets.

For high-risk AI systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, the provider must follow the relevant conformity assessment procedure required under those sector-specific legal acts, with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements incorporated, and only points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and part of 4.6 of Annex VII additionally applying.

Conformity assessment bodies must apply to be designated as notified bodies under Article 29, and only designated bodies may carry out conformity assessments, limited to the activities/types of AI systems for which they are designated.

A 2025 Commission proposal (COM(2025)836) would amend Article 30 to require conformity assessment bodies applying for notified body status to do so according to codes, categories and types of AI systems referenced in a new Annex XIV for the NANDO system, with Commission power to amend these codes.

A Council 'Digital Omnibus on AI' drafting document (deadline 26 February 2026) proposes facilitating notified body designation under both the AI Act and sector-specific legislation via a single application and single assessment procedure, including for bodies already designated under other Union harmonisation legislation.
The NANDO database is the Commission's public information system listing all designated notified bodies, including those for AI Act purposes.

As of 16 December 2025, the NANDO system listed 51 MDR-designated notified bodies and 19 IVDR-designated bodies, with 12 MDR and 6 IVDR designation applications pending (these figures concern medical device regulations, not the AI Act specifically).

As of March 2026, the AI Act notified body designation process was ongoing, with very few bodies fully designated specifically for AI Act conformity assessment; existing notified bodies under other product legislation (e.g., MDR, Machinery Regulation) can assess AI components within their existing scope but AI-specific designation remains limited, described as a bottleneck that the Digital Omnibus aims to address through extended timelines.
Article 35(2) requires the Commission to maintain a publicly accessible, up-to-date list of all notified bodies, including their identification numbers, in the NANDO database.

Under a provision in the consolidated AI Act text (version dated 27 July 2026), the AI Office is to be responsible for conformity assessments and tests of high-risk AI systems subject to third-party conformity assessment under Article 43 before such systems are placed on the market or put into service.

The AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) requires that, for high-risk systems within Annex III, conformity assessment be carried out by a notified body under Article 43 against the obligations of Articles 9–15, including robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15).

Whenever a high-risk AI system undergoes a substantial modification as defined in Article 3(23), it must generally undergo a new conformity assessment, except where modifications are pre-determined and documented.

Via delegated act, the Commission can amend the AI Act so that high-risk AI systems from other critical areas must also undergo third-party conformity assessment where no harmonised standards or common specifications are applied (Article 43(6)).

It is unclear from the sources whether the proposed Digital Omnibus on AI amendments (single application/assessment procedure, new Annex XIV codes) have been formally adopted or remain proposals as of October 2026.
The sources do not clarify the current operational status or membership of the NANDO database specifically for AI Act notified bodies, only general NANDO information and MDR/IVDR/CRA data points.

It is unclear whether the AI Office's role in conducting conformity assessments and tests (per source 13) applies broadly to high-risk AI systems or is limited to a specific category (e.g., GPAI models with systemic risk), and how this interacts with the notified body framework.
The sources do not specify how many Member States have operational national notified-body designation processes in place for the AI Act as of the question date.

It is unclear from the sources what penalties or consequences apply if a high-risk AI system requiring third-party conformity assessment cannot undergo it due to lack of designated notified bodies, beyond the derogation mechanism in Article 46.
The timeline and status of the Annex XIV codes/categories system proposed in COM(2025)836 is not clearly established as adopted or still pending in the sources provided.
report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control (Annex VI) and third-party assessment involving a notified body (Annex VII), with the applicable route depending on the system's category and whether harmonised standards have been applied ([AI Act Service Desk, Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). However, the notified-body ecosystem for AI Act-specific assessments remains underdeveloped, with no source confirming a definitive list of fully AI Act-designated notified bodies as of late 2026, and pending Commission and Council proposals could still reshape the designation process ([COM(2025)836](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025PC0836); [Council WK-3257-2026-INIT](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/WK-3257-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Routes
Article 43 requires providers to follow the Annex VII procedure where harmonised standards or common specifications do not exist or have not been fully applied (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). For high-risk systems under point 1 of Annex III where harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, providers may choose between internal control (Annex VI) or notified-body assessment (Annex VII) (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf); [EU AI Act Key Issue 2](https://www.euaiact.com/key-issue/2)). For most other high-risk systems outside point 1 of Annex III, self-assessment via Annex VI suffices without mandatory third-party certification (low confidence) ([EDPB](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-06/spe-training-on-ai-and-data-protection-legal_en.pdf); [OneTrust](https://www.onetrust.com/blog/what-you-need-to-know-about-conformity-assessments-under-the-eu-ai-act)).

### Annex VII Third-Party Procedure
Annex VII combines evaluation of the provider's quality management system (per Article 17) with review of technical documentation by a notified body (high confidence) ([FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf); [AI Act Service Desk, Article 17](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-17)). Under Annex VII point 4.5, notified bodies may, upon reasoned request and after exhausting other means, gain access to training and trained models, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Annex VII](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). For systems already covered by Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I, Section A), providers follow the sector-specific procedure, with only limited Annex VII points (4.3, 4.4, 4.5, part of 4.6) additionally applying (medium confidence) ([artificialintelligenceact.eu, Article 43](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43)).

### Derogations and Modifications
Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard conformity assessment, authorising temporary market placement for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or critical-infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Article 46](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Substantial modifications generally trigger a new conformity assessment unless pre-determined and documented (low confidence) ([VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

### Notified Body Designation
Conformity assessment bodies must apply under Article 29 and are designated only for specific activities/system types (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Article 29](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-29)). The Commission maintains the NANDO database listing all designated notified bodies, including for AI Act purposes (high confidence) ([NANDO](https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/single-market-compliance-space/notified-bodies)). A 2025 Commission proposal (COM(2025)836) would require applicants to specify codes/categories under a new Annex XIV (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025PC0836)), while a Council draft proposes streamlining designation via a single application process (medium confidence) ([Council WK-3257-2026-INIT](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/WK-3257-2026-INIT/en/pdf)). As of March 2026, very few bodies were specifically designated for AI Act assessments, described as a bottleneck (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on scope: the Futurium "After Mythos" piece generalizes notified-body assessment to all high-risk systems under Annex III (low confidence) ([Futurium, After Mythos](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/after-mythos-why-frontier-ai-conformity-assessment-requires-cryptographic-layer)), whereas Article 43 itself and interpretive sources restrict the optional internal/third-party choice specifically to point 1 of Annex III (low confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43); [Futurium 2021](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf); [EU AI Act Key Issue 2](https://www.euaiact.com/key-issue/2)). A possible discrepancy exists regarding whether the AI Office itself conducts certain conformity assessments (high confidence claim from a 2026 consolidated text) versus the standard notified-body framework—this may reflect an amendment not fully reconciled across sources ([EUR-Lex 2026 text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727); [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). Several low-confidence claims (0.12–0.34) regarding designation counts and substantial-modification rules should be treated cautiously given weak sourcing, including the claim that AI Act-specific notified-body designations remain very limited and bottlenecked as of March 2026 ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)), and the claim that substantial modifications generally trigger a new conformity assessment unless pre-determined and documented ([VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms a current, definitive count of AI Act-specific notified bodies as of October 2026. It remains unclear whether the Digital Omnibus and Annex XIV proposals have been adopted or remain pending. The AI Office's precise role in conformity assessments versus notified bodies is unresolved, as is the consequence of insufficient notified-body capacity beyond Article 46 derogations.

## Methodology Note
This report was produced by an automated research pipeline: web search, source classification, confidence scores computed from source authority, recency and corroboration, and an automated review against the extracted claims.

source_links.notes: Every link points to a gathered source.

citation_coverage.notes: Nearly every factual statement in the report carries an inline markdown citation, including nuanced qualifiers (e.g., 'Several low-confidence claims (0.12–0.34) regarding designation counts and substantial-modification rules...' is sourced to eyreACT and VDE).

hallucination_check.notes: Spot-checked all major factual claims (Annex VII QMS+technical documentation review, Article 46 derogation grounds, Article 29 designation requirement, COM(2025)836 Annex XIV proposal, Council single-application proposal, NANDO database role) against the extracted claims list and found no invented facts, numbers, or dates not present in the ground-truth claims.

contradiction_disclosure.notes: The report's 'Contradictions & Uncertainties' section explicitly surfaces all three known contradictions (scope of Article 43 choice vs. Futurium's 'After Mythos' generalization, the AI Office vs. notified-body role discrepancy, and the unreliable low-confidence designation-count/modification claims), matching the ground-truth contradiction list closely.

confidence_assessment.notes: Confidence labels generally track the underlying scores (e.g., claim_004 0.82→'high confidence', claim_009 0.80→'high confidence', claim_002/003 0.34→'low confidence', claim_013/017/018 0.12→'low confidence'). One minor ambiguity: claim_007 (0.40, derived from authority 0.5) is labeled 'medium confidence' in the report, which sits between the clear low (~0.12-0.34) and medium (~0.68) bands used elsewhere, though this is a defensible borderline call rather than a clear misstatement.

executive_summary_accuracy.notes: The executive summary's claims (two main routes under Annex VI/VII, underdeveloped notified-body ecosystem, lack of a definitive AI Act-specific notified body list as of late 2026, pending Commission/Council proposals) are all substantiated and elaborated upon in the body and knowledge gaps sections.

knowledge_gaps.notes: The 'Knowledge Gaps' section explicitly states the lack of a definitive AI Act notified-body count, uncertainty over adoption status of the Digital Omnibus/Annex XIV proposals, and the unresolved AI Office vs. notified-body role question—closely mirroring the extracted 'Open Issues' list.
